newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kabila says no ceasefire after Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila says no ceasefire after Kisangani.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila proclaimed the fall of Zaire's third city of Kisangani on Saturday and ruled out an immediate ceasefire, saying his forces would "liberate" the whole country.
Kabila told a news conference in the eastern town of Goma that Kisangani and its international airport had been heavily defended but that rebel troops captured the town at 2:45 p.m. (1245 GMT).
"The military commander at the front... said the enemy had crossed the river and we are looking for boats so that we can pursue them," he said.

Kabila, leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, met U.N. envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun, who has been pushing a five-point peace plan which includes an immediate ceasefire.
"Negotiations have to precede a cessation of hostilities," said Kabila, while reaffirming the AFDL's commitment to the principle of the peace plan.
Sahnoun declined to comment as he left the lakeside palace after the talks.
The AFDL has taken control of over a fifth of the vast mineral-rich nation at the heart of Africa since launching its rebellion in October to topple ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kisangani, Zaire's third city and headquarters of a failed government counter offensive, is the biggest rebel prize to date.
"We are still advancing, we must liberate the whole country... we are going everywhere," Kabila said. "To my compatriots I ask them to remain calm in the knowledge that the AFDL is advancing."
Kabila said he was still in favour of negotiations with Mobutu if he is willing to take part in person.
"If they agree to being present at the negotiating table that may constitute some kind of pause," he said. "If they don't negotiate they will be forced with military action to negotiate or to flee."
Kabila said Mobutu's ragged army was buttresed in Kisangani by Hutu soldiers of the former Rwandan army, Angolan UNITA rebels, foreign mercenaries and French advisors.
He said soldiers of Mobutu's Special Presidential Division, together with some mercenaries, had taken flight to the central diamond-mining city of Mbuji Mayi and set up a new headquarters.

Kabila said the AFDL would continue to provide access and security for humanitarian agencies trying to look after hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees, but did not rule out a move in the direction of their main camp at Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani.
"We haven't moved in that direction, but it is part of our country, as long as there are armed groups and mercenaries in that area we will have to move towards them," Kabila said.

Hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutus fled the rebel advance from camps further east, fearing reprisals from ethnic Tutsis among the rebel force for Rwanda's 1994 genocide by Hutu hardliners of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
